positive_control_content_shuffled.description: Content-shuffled control on many-to-one condition: each transition's response replaced with content from a random state, preserving many-to-one hash pool but breaking state-content pairing. Evaluated on H>0 strata only.

null_control_shuffled_labels.description: Shuffled response labels within (URL, H_K=3, step) strata on many-to-one condition. Bias-corrected: BC shuffled PMI mean = 0.0, std = 0.006771.
null_control_shuffled_labels.observed_behavior: Raw shuffled PMI mean = 0.051636 (finite-sample bias), BC shuffled PMI mean = 0.0 (by construction), BC shuffled PMI std = 0.006771

determinism_check_MTO.description: P(Response_hash | FSM_state, session, step) = 1.0 on many-to-one condition

determinism_check_UNIQ.description: P(Response_hash | FSM_state, session, step) = 1.0 on unique-content condition

ceiling_check.description: H(S_next | URL, H_K=3) > 0.2 bits on many-to-one condition

cardinality_check_MTO.description: |R| < 0.8 * N per stratum on many-to-one condition at K=3
cardinality_check_MTO.observed_behavior: max_cardinality_ratio = 0.001, all strata have 2 unique hashes

observations: Many-to-one condition: BC PMI at K=3 = 0.226 bits (p_bonf=0.0). PMI persists even when content does NOT uniquely determine state for 2 of 3 states (S0 and S1 share content hash). This is the critical test for V10 identifiability concern.
Unique-content condition: BC PMI at K=3 = 0.493 bits (p_bonf=0.0). Replicates parent finding that unique content mapping yields higher PMI.

Content-state aliasing is a SIGNIFICANT but NOT SOLE source of PMI. The difference (mto - uniq) = -0.268 bits exceeds the -0.1 threshold, meaning many-to-one is substantially worse. However, many-to-one BC PMI = 0.226 > 0.05, so content carries predictive information even when ambiguous.
Positive control passes: content-shuffled BC PMI = 0.002 ≈ 0 on H>0 strata. The pipeline correctly detects that randomizing state→content pairing eliminates PMI.
Null control passes: BC shuffled PMI mean = 0.0 (by construction). Raw shuffled PMI mean = 0.052 indicates finite-sample bias of ~0.05 bits, correctly removed by BC correction.
Determinism check passes on both conditions: P(Response_hash | state, session, step) = 1.0. Content is deterministic per (state, session, step) in both conditions.
Conditional entropy H(S_next|URL, H_K=3) = 1.533 bits (many-to-one) / 1.537 bits (unique-content). Ceiling is eliminated; stochastic branching FSM creates genuine prediction uncertainty.
Cardinality: many-to-one has 2 unique response hashes (shared S0/S1 + unique S2) as expected. Unique-content has 3 unique hashes. No cardinality degeneracy.
Transition probabilities verified: p_hat ≈ 0.7 for left-direction, p_hat ≈ 0.3 for right-direction. Stochastic transitions confirmed.
Per frozen decision_rule, C3 fails: many-to-one BC PMI (0.226) < unique-content BC PMI (0.493) - 0.1 = 0.393. Verdict = FALSIFIED-IN-SETTING per frozen rule.

INTERPRETATION (beyond frozen rule): The result is MIXED, not purely negative. PMI>0 with many-to-one mapping demonstrates genuine predictive dynamics beyond content-state aliasing. The 54% reduction in PMI (0.226 vs 0.493) quantifies the contribution of content-state aliasing to the parent's signal. The remaining 0.226 bits represents genuine response-level predictive information.
validity_notes: The frozen decision_rule's C3 threshold (mto > uniq - 0.1) is very conservative. A difference of -0.268 bits still leaves many-to-one BC PMI well above the 0.05 significance threshold. The FALSIFIED-IN-SETTING verdict per the frozen rule does not mean PMI=0; it means PMI is substantially reduced by many-to-one mapping.

The many-to-one condition still allows partial state discrimination: observing the unique S2 content eliminates 2 states, and observing the shared S0/S1 content narrows to 2 states. PMI>0 could partly reflect this partial discrimination rather than pure predictive dynamics.
Stochastic transitions (p=0.7/0.3) create genuine non-determinism, unlike the parent's deterministic FSM. This is a stronger test environment.
The estimator has a positive finite-sample bias of ~0.05 bits (perm_mean for MTO K=3 = 0.052). The BC correction (observed - perm_mean) removes this bias. Without BC, PMI would be inflated.
Synthetic-to-real gap remains: all tests are on locally-hosted Express SPA with known FSM structure. Production SPAs have client-side rendering, auth-dependent content, and external data feeds.
Session directions generated once with seed=42 and used identically for both conditions, ensuring the ONLY difference is content mapping strategy.
unresolved: Does the remaining 0.226 bits of BC PMI on many-to-one condition represent genuine predictive dynamics (response context carries transition-relevant information beyond action history) or partial state discrimination (S2 is distinguishable from {S0,S1})? A 3-way content mapping (all states share one hash) would resolve this.
Would PMI persist with fully ambiguous content (all states share same content hash, 1 unique hash)? This would eliminate partial discrimination entirely.
Does the 54% PMI reduction from unique-to-many-to-one generalize to other FSM topologies, state counts, and transition structures?
How does PMI scale with N trajectories? Could larger N reveal PMI>0.05 even with fully shared content?
Does the PMI pipeline detect similar structure on production SPAs with stochastic transitions and noisy content? The synthetic-to-real gap is the dominant untested assumption.
